rv.q: Hungry Women is hardly starved for material, and serves up a playwright ravished with talent and voracious in ambition.
The playwright and director Daniella Caggiano have done a surprisingly good job of managing all the moving parts within an overall logical framework...
The performances by Julia Lester, Zoe Dean, Mariyea and Sophie Zmorrod are riveting enough to supersede this dramaturgical problem.
Like costume designer Olivia Vaughn Hern’s corsets, Hungry Women has good bones.
If “Hungry Women” is plainly the work of a novice, and something of a slog, it shows a ravenous imagination.
Hungry Women remains an imaginative, sharply written satire that refuses easy answers.
I encourage all who are hungry for big questions about gender and cruelty to come to SoHo Playhouse and take a bite.
However, Maney and the play’s director, Daniella Caggiano, never quite settle on a tone, confusing the audience and undercutting the play’s deceptively straightforward message...
Hungry Women promises an exciting and unique feast but ends up serving unsatisfying grub.

cn.t: Maney's dystopian premise of a male-free world across three time periods intrigues critics, but the execution proves uneven. Most find the sci-fi concept compelling and performances strong, though the play struggles to balance its tonal ambitions.

vr.q: Hungry Women is going to be a Broadway Ben recommendation.
The slight tonal whiplash ended up feeling justified by the insightful concept that encompassed. I had one of the most intriguing post show conversations I've had in a while.
